news.text: You come back with a look I do not like. Speak.

choices.text: Your brother is alive, Majesty. He lives at the Greywatch.

alive.text: You lie.” His gloved hand closes into a fist. “I saw that tower burn. I went into the fire after him and found nothing.

choices.text: He crawled out through the cellar. Wynn Hollis found him on the west road.

cellar.text: Nothing… because there was nothing to find.” He sits down heavily on the dais step. “Thirty-one years I have kept that door shut, because opening it meant saying what we did. Did he say anything of me?

choices.text: He said he never blamed the boy.
He said the door can be opened now.

forgive.text: Then it will be opened. At first light, before the whole town, and the granary filled again as Aldra meant it. And then I will ride to the Greywatch myself.” He pulls off the glove and looks at the old scar. “By bridge and by bread, traveller. Thank you.
forgive.leave: Bow, and leave the brothers their peace.

after.text: The smith is cutting the chains at dawn. I have not slept. I find I do not mind.

choices.text: Will you go to the Greywatch?

ride.text: Tomorrow. Alone, without a crown. I owe him a winter's worth of bread and thirty-one years of apology, and I mean to start with the bread.

greet.text: A traveller in my hall, unannounced. Few are so bold these days. Speak, and be brief.

choices.text: Forgive me, Your Majesty. I came to see Valdren.
Why do you wear only one glove?
I will leave you in peace.

again.text: You again. Ask what you came to ask.

choices.text: Tell me of the Red Winter.
Why do you wear only one glove?

kingdom.text: Then look well. Queen Aldra raised the bridge, my forefathers raised these walls, and I keep them standing. Three hundred and two years, and no army has ever crossed that river uninvited.

choices.text: In the town they speak of a Red Winter.

aldra.text: The founder. A ferryman's daughter who bridged the river and swore an oath on its first stone: ‘By bridge and by bread.’ It is woven into every banner in this hall, though few remember what it means.

choices.text: Tell me of your father, King Harald.
I have taken enough of your time.

oath.text: That the crown holds the kingdom's grain in trust, and opens its stores to the hungry in a hard year. A fine promise. Promises are cheaper than granaries.

choices.text: Was it kept in the Red Winter?

redwinter.text: The year the harvest rotted in the fields and the frost came early. I was young. My father held the realm together while lesser men panicked. That is all the chronicles need to say.

harald.text: Harald the Steadfast. His statue stands in the market so that no one forgets who saved Valdren. He was a hard man. Hard winters need hard men.

granary.text: Open it? It was guarded. There were armies on the far bank and spies in every inn. A king who feeds his enemies loses his kingdom. We did what had to be done.

choices.text: And your brother? What did he do?

starved.text: You speak of things you did not see. I saw them. Leave it there, traveller.

glove.text: A burn. An old one. A king's hand should not tremble in public, so I keep it covered. You are bold to ask.

burn.text: A fire, thirty years ago, in a tower at the edge of the forest. I was too slow. We will not speak of it again.

edmund.text: Edmund. My elder brother died in the Greywatch fire, killed by brigands. The chronicles say so. The stone in the old burial ground says so.

edmund2.text: I say he was braver than I was, and more foolish, and that the door he opened has stayed shut ever since.

choices.text: Then I will leave you to your memories.

door.text: The door in the donjon. My father had it chained the morning after the fire, and I have never had it opened. Some doors are graves too. Go now.

greet.text: Halt. You're not one of mine. State your business in the king's yard.

choices.text: I'd like an audience with the king.

again.text: Back again? Walk with me if you're talking. I've a round to finish.

choices.text: What does the guard watch for?

traveller.text: Travellers are welcome in Valdren, so long as their hands stay where I can see them. Isolde Varn, Captain of the Guard, as my father was before me.

choices.text: What does the guard watch for?
I'll keep my hands in sight.

audience.text: The hall's straight ahead, and the king's mood is about as warm as the river in January. Mind your tongue in there.

watch.text: Cutpurses on market days, drunks at the Broken Oar, wolves on the west road. And the old ruin by the forest, though there's nothing left in it but a hermit and bad memories.

greywatch.text: That was the Greywatch, Prince Edmund's tower. It burned in the Red Winter with the prince inside it. Brigands, the chronicle says. My father never said brigands. He never said anything at all.

choices.text: I'll let you get back to your round.

hermit.text: Old man with a staff and a burned face. Lives by the ruin, comes to market twice a year, pays in honey. Harmless. The farm widow walks bread out to him.

father.text: Captain Aldous Varn. Led the guard thirty years and died last winter. Something weighed on him all that time. He drank to it every year, on the same night.

sorry.text: Don't be. He had a long life and a short temper. Now, unless you need something, I've a gate to watch.

night.text: Aye. After the funeral I found a letter in his chest, the royal seal broken on it. An order to arrest Prince Edmund. ‘Bring him alive,’ it said. Arrest, not rescue. Keep that to yourself.

order.text: King Harald's seal. And beneath it, the name of the officer who rode with my father to carry it out: Prince Osric. Our king.

greet.text: Mind the sparks. If you're buying, I've nails, hinges and a decent knife. If you're gawping, gawp from over there.

choices.text: Have you always been the smith here?
Tell me again about the donjon door.
Your family made every lock in Valdren?

forging.text: Hinges for the Town Hall door. The council meets twice a year, and every time those old hinges scream like a scalded cat.

choices.text: Have you always been the smith here?

family.text: Four generations at this anvil. My father, his father, and his before that. Every lock and chain in Valdren came out of this forge.

castle.text: Gate hinges, portcullis teeth, the guards' mail. And the chains on the donjon door, though that was my father's work, not mine.

chains.text: He forged them in a single night, the night after the Greywatch burned, with soldiers standing over him till dawn. He only spoke of it once, in his cups: ‘I locked bread away from hungry people.’

bread.text: The royal granary is under the donjon. Has been since Queen Aldra's day. If there's grain in there after thirty years it's dust and rats. But that winter it was full. Full.

why.text: Ask the king, if you've the nerve. All I know is the lock has no key. My father melted it in this forge, on royal orders.

greet.text: Welcome to the Broken Oar! Ale's brown, stew's hot, and the gossip's free. What'll it be, love?

name.text: Before the bridge there was a ferry, and the ferryman was Aldra's father. When she built the bridge she broke his oar over the first stone, so no one would ever pay to cross again. Or so my grandmother told it.

gossip.text: Let's see. The smith's sweet on the miller's sister, the Town Hall hinges scream, and the king hasn't smiled since my mother was a girl.

king.text: Lost his brother young. Prince Edmund, the one the old folk still raise a cup to when they think nobody's watching. Edmund of the Carts, they called him.

carts.text: In the Red Winter, the story goes, he fed half the valley off the back of grain carts. Ask old Wynn at the farm. She was there; I was a babe in arms.

songs.text: There's one. Not one I'd sing loud, mind; the guard broke a fiddler's fingers for it once. But you've an honest face.

ballad.text: ♪ The king kept the bread in his tower of stone, / the prince drove the carts down the frost-bitten road; / they burned the grey watch with the prince in its keep, / but the valley remembers, and the valley won't sleep. ♪

writer.text: Nobody knows. Some say a farm girl. Some say the hermit out by the ruin, though he's never once set foot in here. Pays in honey at the market, they tell me.
writer.leave: Leave a coin on the bench.

greet.text: Cloth from the coast, pepper from beyond the sea, needles finer than a lady's eyelash! Ah, a new face. Tobias Fenn, at your service.

again.text: Back for pepper? No? Then for gossip, which is cheaper.

choices.text: Tell me about the bridge stone.

outsider.text: Saltmere, three weeks downriver. I come up every spring. Valdren's bridge is the only crossing for forty miles, so sooner or later everyone comes through here.

trade.text: Good, if you don't mind the king's tolls. Better than thirty years ago, my father would say. Back then grain sold for silver by the cup.

bridge.text: The bridge is the whole kingdom! No bridge, no road, no market, no Valdren. There's a stone at its south end with Queen Aldra's oath on it. Merchants touch it for luck.

choices.text: I'll go and touch it myself.

oath.text: ‘Ponte et pane’: by bridge and by bread. The crown keeps the crossing open and the granary full, and in a hungry year the granary opens to all. That bargain is why the farmers swore to her.

kept.text: Ha! Ask the farmers about the Red Winter. Up and down the river they still say ‘tight as Harald's granary’. My father traded here that year. He said the castle had grain and the town had funerals.

greet.text: Mind the furrows, they're new. If you're from the castle, the levy's paid. If you're not, well, hello.

again.text: Back again? Grab a hoe or grab a seat.

choices.text: Tell me about the Red Winter.

letter.text: She told me to burn it. I never could.” She leans on the hoe. “Then you know I was nineteen and foolish and brave, once. Keep it to yourself, or don't. I'm too old to be frightened of the castle now.

notcastle.text: Then sit a moment; my knees want an excuse. Name's Wynn. My family has farmed this bank since before the bridge.

choices.text: Do you remember the Red Winter?

harvest.text: Good enough. Wheat's tall, barley's fat, and the mill's turning. I never complain about good years. I've seen the other kind.

redwinter.text: I was nineteen. Blight in the summer, frost in the autumn, and by midwinter we were boiling bark. My little brother didn't see the spring. Nor did half the babes in the valley.

castle.text: The castle shut its gates. Then one night, in the deep of winter, there were carts on the road. Grain carts, with the prince's own riders walking beside them.

edmund.text: Edmund himself, his hands raw from the reins. He opened his father's granary without asking and gave it away sack by sack. Three nights later his tower was burning.

after.text: The chronicles say he died.” She looks west, towards the forest. “I bake an extra loaf on Fridays. Old habit. Don't ask me who eats it.

truth.text: You have the look of someone who has been reading old stones. Well? Out with it.

choices.text: I know who you are. Edmund of the Carts.

confess.text: Edmund.” He is quiet for a long time. “Nobody has said that name to my face in thirty-one years. Aye. I opened my father's granary because Aldra's oath said I must, and because children were dying. They came to arrest me, my brother with them, and the fire came too. I crawled out through the cellar. Wynn found me on the road.

choices.text: Why did you never go back?
Your brother has blamed himself ever since.

why.text: Go back to what? A father who would have hanged me, and a kingdom ready to split in two over which son to follow. One dead prince was cheaper than a war. And the valley ate that winter. That was enough for me.

choices.text: Your brother has blamed himself ever since.

brother.text: Has he.” He looks down at his scarred hands. “Then tell him. Tell him the door can be opened now; there's no one left behind it to starve. And tell him I never blamed the boy.

after.text: Did you tell him? No, don't answer. I'll know soon enough if he comes.

come.text: Then I had better find a second cup.” For the first time in a long while, he laughs. “Go on, now.

greet.text: Hm. A visitor. Mind the fire, and mind the stones; the tower drops one now and then, to remind me it's still angry.

again.text: Back by my fire? Sit, then. The crows are poor company.

choices.text: Tell me about the night the tower burned.
Who leaves heather on the prince's grave?

who.text: Nobody. An old man who keeps bees and talks to crows. The crows are better listeners.

choices.text: I'll leave you to your crows.

scar.text: Fire is a careless sculptor.” He turns his cheek from the light. “Ask about the living, traveller. The burned have nothing to tell you.

place.text: The Greywatch. It guarded the west road once, when Valdren still had something to guard it against. Now it guards me, and does a poor job of it.

burned.text: In the Red Winter. Thirty-one years ago this winter. Brigands, they say in the town.

choices.text: It wasn't brigands. It was the king's guard.
The prince's grave is empty. Even the song says so.

then.text: I have always been here, or it feels so. Go and talk to the living: the smith, the farm wife, the Captain. When you know more, come and tell me what you've learned.

guard.text: Did they now.” He is quiet a long while. “Then you've spoken to a Varn. Old Aldous kept his silence longer than anyone deserved.

varn.text: He carried an order he hated, from a king he feared, with a boy beside him who wanted to be anywhere else. The boy kicked in the door. The guard brought torches. Nobody meant the fire. Fire rarely asks.

osric.text: The boy ran into the flames after his brother and came out with his hand on fire and nothing in it. He has carried that empty hand ever since.” He stirs the embers. “Tell no one I said so.

grave.text: Is it.” He smiles, and it doesn't reach his eyes. “Then whoever lies there is lighter than me, and luckier.

heather.text: Heather grows wild on the ridge. An old man walks; an old man picks. The dead don't mind.

deny.text: Edmund of the Carts died in this tower with his father's bread on his conscience. I'm only the hermit who keeps his bees.” He looks at you a long while. “If you want the rest, find what the kingdom hid: the stones, the scrolls, the door. Then come back.

greet.text: Halt. Oh, just a traveller. Welcome to Valdren. Keep your blade sheathed and your purse closer.

greet.text: Pull up a bench, stranger. The ale's honest and the company's… well, it's me.

again.text: Back for another? Good lad. Good lass. Good whoever you are.

choices.text: What do you think of the king?

t1.text: The aeronauts are back from Saltmere with a red-and-gold balloon. Biggest one yet, they say.

choices.text: What do you think of the king?

t2.text: I think the king's a sad man in a big hall. Maera says he never smiles. Neither would I, with that crown on.

greet.text: Mm? Oh, hello. Don't mind me, I'm waiting for my husband. He's been ‘just one more minute’ for an hour.

t0.text: Arguing about horses at the stables, most likely. If you see a red-faced man shouting about hooves, that's my Godric.

t1.text: Maera's stew is the best in the valley. With Hilde's bread it's better still.

greet.text: To the traveller! May your boots stay dry and your cup stay full.

t0.text: Wool. I trade it. The sheep do the hard part; I do the talking.

t1.text: Stone, cold, full of ledgers. The clock on its tower keeps better time than the council does.

greet.text: Fresh loaves! Rye, barley, honey bread. Oh, a new face! Welcome, welcome.

again.text: Back for more? The honey bread's just out.

t0.text: Made with honey from the old beekeeper out west. He trades it at the market. Best honey in the valley, and he never says a word more than he must.

t1.text: Those rascals at the fountain? They bring me luck. And they buy the burnt ends for a farthing.

t2.text: Better than ever. A bigger town means more mouths, and every mouth wants bread.

greet.text: The Town Hall is open to every citizen. Mind the ledgers; some are older than the bridge.

t0.text: The council meets, argues, and writes it all down. I write it down twice.

t1.text: Made by a clockmaker from Saltmere. It strikes nothing and rings nothing; it simply keeps the time. The council likes it that way.

t2.text: The council of guilds, under the Crown. The king rarely comes down from the castle these days.

greet.text: Apples! Pears! Plums from the south orchards! Taste one, go on.

again.text: Changed your mind about those plums?

t0.text: For you? Free. Tell your friends, and they'll pay double.

t1.text: Orchards past the river, beyond the farms. Wynn Hollis grows the best pears, though don't tell her I said so.

greet.text: Ribbons, flowers, wooden toys! Something for the little ones?

again.text: Back again? The wooden balloons are going fast.

t0.text: Carved by my father: horses, ducks, a little balloon on a string. The children love the balloon.

t1.text: The balloon festival! The aeronauts fly over the town every summer, and we deck the streets for them.

greet.text: Hear ye, hear ye! News of Valdren, fresh as Hilde's bread!

choices.text: Tell me again about the cutpurse.

t1.text: The castle keeps its own counsel, traveller. I cry what I'm paid to cry.

t2.text: Through the east gate and along the cart track. You can't miss them; they're the size of houses!

case1_w.text: The cutpurse? Saw him plain as day! A skinny young fellow, no beard, a green hat with a red feather, and a patched brown cloak. Cut a purse off a farmer's belt by the stalls and strolled off as if he owned the market. He'll be back; that sort always is.

choices.text: A green hat and a brown cloak. Thank you.

case1_w2.text: Round the stalls, where the purses are fattest. Look for the hat, but mind: half of Valdren wears a hat, and Tobias the merchant has a green one too. Check the cloak, and the chin.

greet.text: Easy there, don't spook the horses. They're shy of strangers.

t1.text: Town horses, mostly: the carters', the council's, and one old warhorse the Captain retired.

greet.text: The grey is worth twice what they're asking, I tell you! Twice!

Your wife is waiting at the Broken Oar.

t1.text: Thirty years a carter. I know a sound hoof when I see one.

t2.text: My crew from Saltmere. We drift with the wind and land wherever the farmers are friendliest.

t0.text: Perch, pike, and once an eel as long as my arm that bit the boy who caught it.

t1.text: Deep enough that nobody's found the bottom in the middle. Grandfather said there's a sunken ship out there full of salt.

case2_w.text: I was out before dawn and saw a rowing boat slip in to the quay, no lantern. The man at the oars wore a grey cowl, and when he turned there was a scar right across his cheek. Went off with a barrel on his shoulder like it weighed nothing.

choices.text: A grey cowl and a scar. Thank you.

case2_w2.text: Along the quay. He works the docks, I'd swear to it. There's more than one grey cowl on this quay, mind; it's cold before dawn. Look for the scar.

greet.text: Ahoy! You've the look of someone who's never been to sea. Lucky you.

t0.text: Saltmere, the islands past it, and once all the way to the edge of the map, where the cook nearly started a mutiny.

t1.text: I wish! I only haul her ropes. Her captain has a green coat and a voice like a foghorn.

greet.text: Shh! You'll scare the fish.

t0.text: Two little ones and a boot. The boot was the biggest.

t1.text: Loads of times! She flies over the lighthouse when the sun goes down. One day I'll ride her.

greet.text: Welcome to the light. A hundred and eighty steps to the top, and I climb them twice a day.

t0.text: Brings the night boats home across Mirrormere. The lake is calm, but the rocks under the north shore are not.

choices.text: Do you see the dragon from up there?

t1.text: Most evenings. She breathes fire at the clouds, then circles the light three times as if she's checking it's still lit. I've grown fond of her.

t2.text: I have the gulls, the ships, the dragon and the stars. Lonely is a town full of people who never look up.

choices.text: Do you see the dragon from up there?

greet.text: Welcome to the Millstone! Warm fire, cold ale, and the best mutton pie south of the river.

choices.text: Do you go to the town?

again.text: Another pie? I'll put it on your tab. You don't have a tab. You do now.

choices.text: Do you go to the town?

t0.text: Twenty houses, one well, one pond, too many ducks and not enough husbands. Ask anyone.

choices.text: Do you go to the town?

t1.text: Every market day, with pies. Hilde and I trade: my pies for her honey bread. Best bargain in the valley.

greet.text: Sit a while. The green doesn't charge.

t0.text: I was born in that house there, and I'll die on this bench if the ducks let me.

t1.text: The Hollis girl's pears are the best in years, the pond's full of ducks again, and someone saw the dragon over the south hills.

case3_w.text: Saw him, I did, from this very bench. Big as a barn door, red beard down to here, a straw hat, and a sack over his shoulder that was bleating. Bleating! He went off down the lane as if he'd every right.

choices.text: Red beard and a straw hat. Thank you.

case3_w2.text: Me? I'm part of the bench by now. Half the village wears a straw hat in summer, mind. Look for the beard.

greet.text: Steady now, they spook easy. Sheep are mostly fear held together with wool.

choices.text: Do you lose sheep to the dragon?
How many sheep do you keep?

again.text: Counted them again. Got a different number again.

t0.text: One a year, maybe. She leaves a gold coin where it stood, every time. I've four in a jar. Best bargain I ever made.

choices.text: How many sheep do you keep?

t1.text: Eight here and eleven on the east meadow. I count them every night and get a different number every time.

greet.text: Welcome to the Wardens' Guild. We keep the peace the castle guard is too grand to bother with: cutpurses, smugglers, rustlers. The crown pays a bounty for every one we bring in, and you look like you can handle yourself.

choices.text: Have you any work for me?

how.text: Take a case from the board and ask the witness what they saw. Then find whoever matches it, and look closely: faces, beards, hats and cloaks. Name them to their face and they'll run. Catch them and beat them till they yield, bind their hands, and bring them here to me. And don't thump the wrong person. The guards fine brawlers.

reward.text: Crowns, paid the moment you hand a culprit over. Spend them at the market. Brannoc at the forge sells a steel sword that's worth every one.

offer1.text: Here's one. Purses are being cut at the market, in broad daylight, bold as you like. Bartholomew the crier saw the thief make off. Twenty-five crowns if you bring him in.

took1.text: Good. Talk to Bartholomew; he cries the news from the middle of the market. And watch your own purse.

choices.text: Mark the market on my map.

on1.text: Any luck with the cutpurse? Bartholomew the crier saw him, in the market.

choices.text: Mark the market on my map.

hand1.text: Well, well. The market cutpurse. You look smaller up close, Wat.

paid1.text: Into the cells with him. Twenty-five crowns, as promised; you earned every one. Come back when you want more work.

choices.text: What else is on the board?

offer2.text: A harder one. Barrels of Saltmere wine keep vanishing off the night boats at Aldra's Haven, on the lake. Smuggling, under the harbour master's nose. Nessa the fisherwoman is out before dawn; she may have seen something. Forty crowns.

took2.text: The harbour's a long way east, past the balloon meadow. Smugglers fight dirty, so keep your blade handy.

choices.text: Mark the harbour on my map.

on2.text: The smuggler? Talk to Nessa the fisherwoman at Aldra's Haven.

choices.text: Mark the harbour on my map.

hand2.text: Silas Marr! Two summers I've been after you. Fine work, traveller.

paid2.text: Forty crowns. The harbour master will sleep better, and so will I.

offer3.text: One more, and the worst. Someone's stealing sheep from Hob's flock and driving them south through Millbrook. A big brute, they say, and he won't come quietly. Old Tom sits on the Millbrook green all day; if anyone saw him, Tom did. Fifty-five crowns.

took3.text: Millbrook's south, over the old bridge and past the farms. Eat something first; I hear he hits hard.

on3.text: The sheep thief? Old Tom on the Millbrook green may have seen him.

hand3.text: Dunstan Rook. Hob will want his sheep back, and the crown wants you. Splendid work, traveller.

paid3.text: Fifty-five crowns, and the guild's thanks. That clears the board, thanks to you. Valdren's a quieter place for it.

cleared.text: The board is clear: cutpurse, smuggler and sheep thief, all in the cells. Valdren owes you, and the guild won't forget it.

choices.text: How did it all work, again?

lag.text: You've bound them? Good. Now bring them here, right beside me, and I'll take them off your hands.

greet.text: Afternoon, friend! Lovely day for the market. Lots of folk about. Lots of… busy folk.

choices.text: You seem very taken with people's belts.
Green hat, brown cloak, smooth chin. You're the cutpurse, Wat. The guild wants you.

again.text: You again? I've done nothing. Nothing at all.

choices.text: Green hat, brown cloak, smooth chin. You're the cutpurse, Wat. The guild wants you.

t0.text: Belts? No, no. I like looking at the… fruit. Lovely fruit, Jory has.

t1.text: Here and there. Mostly there. Ask anyone. Well, don't ask anyone. Ask me, and I'll tell you: there.

choices.text: You seem very taken with people's belts.

accuse.text: The guild? Ha! You'll have to catch me first, and nobody's ever caught Wat Nimble!

caught.text: You again! I'm not going to any guild!

greet.text: Buttons, buckles, bootlaces! Perkin Ashe, pedlar, at your service.

choices.text: A hat, a cloak, no beard. You're the cutpurse, aren't you?

again.text: Changed your mind about the bootlaces?

t0.text: Seen? I've lost a purse myself this week! A skinny lad brushed past me by the fruit stall, and when I looked, my purse was gone.

t1.text: Never saw his face. A hat, I think, but green or brown? Everything's green in spring.

accuse.text: Me?! Look at me: a brown hat, a green cloak, and I'm the one who's been robbed! Ask the crier who he saw; it wasn't me.

greet.text: What d'you want? Can't you see I'm working?

t0.text: Barrels, crates, sacks. Whatever comes off the boats. I don't ask what's in them.

t1.text: Who works nights? Nobody works nights. Boats don't come in at night.

accuse.text: Clever, aren't you? Not clever enough to catch me!

caught.text: Still sniffing after me? You'll have to run for it!

greet.text: Mind the nets, traveller. I've only just mended them.

choices.text: A grey cowl on the docks before dawn. Is it you smuggling the wine?

t0.text: I sleep at night, like an honest man. Though I've heard oars, before dawn, when the boats should all be in.

t1.text: Half the town. The loud ones, the quiet ones. The quiet ones you want to watch.

accuse.text: Me? With my knees? Look at my face, young one. Not a mark on it but the wrinkles. Whoever Nessa saw, it wasn't me.

greet.text: Hrm. Who're you, then?

choices.text: A big man with a red beard and a straw hat, with a sack that bleats. You're the sheep thief, Dunstan.

t0.text: Cattle, mostly. Sheep, sometimes. Whatever needs driving. Why?

t1.text: Here and there. South. Further south. Never you mind.

accuse.text: Sheep thief, am I? Then come and take me, if you can!

caught.text: Back for another go? Come on, then!

greet.text: Mind the ladder. Half the roofs in Millbrook leak, and I'm the only thatcher.

t0.text: Hob's lost six this month, and he's fit to be tied. Someone's driving them south by night.

t1.text: There's a big drover come up from the south this summer. Loud. Never buys a round.

accuse.text: Me? Everyone wears a straw hat in summer! And look: not a whisker on my chin. Ask Tom who he saw.
